issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The rest of the presentation centers on assault-related fear, hypervigilance, restricted safety, intrusive memories, and alcohol/drug use or mental rehearsal as coping. Physical self-harm introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not supported elsewhere in the triggers, threat, appraisal, or memory items, making the strategy set less coherent.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost my connection to my community and culture' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and demographics as presented. The other appraisal items are highly individual and interpersonal ('can't rely on myself', 'permanently an outsider now'), but this item specifically implies a cultural/community rupture that is not otherwise reflected in the triggers, threat items, or other appraisals. Given the provided demographic context, it reads as insufficiently grounded rather than clearly linked to the rest of this sexual-assault formulation.

vignette: Margaret is a 69-year-old agricultural worker who has spent decades harvesting crops in rural California. The trauma happened five years ago, when a younger coworker she had trusted cornered her in a storage shed after a long day. He assaulted her while she pleaded for him to stop, and afterward she told no one, certain she would be blamed. She left that farm and found work at another, hoping the memory would fade, but it did not. The memory surfaced without warning—while she rode the bus to work, the sight of a man in a similar cap brought the shed back vividly. Buses became a trigger, as did any conversation about workplace safety or male kindness, which made the shame feel fresh. When these triggers hit, Margaret’s immediate response was to reach for alcohol. She would pour a glass of wine as soon as she got home, or she would sit and mentally rehearse the worst possible outcomes of her day—preparing herself for another attack so she wouldn’t be caught off guard. She also began avoiding people entirely, canceling plans with friends and skipping church. The triggers also stirred up intense threat reactions. After a memory intruded, she would find herself looking behind her constantly, checking if someone was following, even in the grocery store. Her heart would race, and she felt a mix of fear and guilt—fear of another attack, guilt that she hadn’t fought back. She came to believe she could not rely on herself; after all, she had frozen during the assault, and now she couldn’t control her own mind. Margaret felt like a permanent outsider, set apart from others who had not experienced such violation. This sense of isolation made her especially sensitive to any conversational topic that touched on vulnerability, which would then trigger another intrusive memory, cementing the cycle. Her negative appraisals drove her maladaptive strategies directly. Because she believed she could not rely on herself, she rehearsed worst-case scenarios obsessively, trying to be ready. And because she saw herself as an outsider, avoidance felt natural—why expose herself to more judgment? But the strategies backfired. The mental rehearsal often brought the original assault to mind in vivid detail, acting as its own trigger. Drinking dulled her vigilance but then left her feeling vulnerable, which increased her perception of threat. Carrying that constant sense of threat, she found that even harmless sights—a figure in the distance, a door left ajar—now registered as warnings. Avoidance meant that when she did have to go out—to work, to the pharmacy—her anxiety was sky-high, and she would scan her surroundings constantly. Scanning for danger itself became a trigger: catching a glimpse of a man who looked like her attacker would flood the memory back. Now Margaret’s world has shrunk. She only feels safe in her own home and her daughter’s house. Her husband drives her to work because she can no longer tolerate the bus. She has stopped attending family gatherings, afraid a conversation will bring the shame to the surface. Last week, a neighbor made a casual comment about “looking over your shoulder,” and Margaret broke down sobbing. That night she drank more than usual and could not sleep. Her husband urged her to see a doctor, and she agreed, though she is terrified that talking about the assault will only make the memories worse. She hopes, somewhere, that there might be a way to feel less like an outsider, but she is not sure she can trust herself to get better.
